prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layered layout: the hanging garments occupy the near foreground, roughly 0.2–0.8 m from the camera wearer, while the slat wall and upper background are farther away, approximately 1–3 m. Across frames 1–3, the nearest garment shifts from the left/centre toward the centre-right and grows brighter, indicating approach; in frames 4–5, a very near person or garment enters from the right and expands until it occludes most of the scene, likely within about 0.1–0.4 m. The central grey shirt remains in front of the wall at roughly arm’s reach, with the camera wearer’s hand/arm approaching it from the right in frames 3–4; near surfaces overlap farther wall regions, but fine separations between the hand, person, and clothing are poorly resolved. This relative near/far structure is clearer than in RGB alone, but metric distances are only rough because the map has smooth, merged boundaries, frame-to-frame scale changes, and likely treats similarly shaped people and garments as continuous depth surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates several foreground regions but identifies them unreliably: a large left-side hanging garment in frame 1 is labelled “person,” a narrow partial region at the right edge of frame 2 is also labelled as a person, and the prominent diagonal garment or structural edge in frame 2 is labelled “knife.” In frame 3, small regions appear near the top edge and a person-labelled vertical region occupies the right side; in frame 4 another partial person mask enters from the right, and in frame 5 a very large person-labelled mask fills nearly the entire frame while another narrow person region remains at the far right. The masks make changing occlusion explicit: foreground regions expand from limited left/right-edge coverage to almost total blockage by frame 5, showing that something comes very close to the camera and hides the wall and garments behind it. The map does not provide metric distance or dependable facing direction, and its class labels and boundaries conflict with the RGB enough that object identity, inter-person distance, and whether anyone looks toward the camera cannot be trusted.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects no body or hands in frames 1–2, then shows a compact body-and-hand cluster in the right half of frame 3 and a hand-only cluster farther right in frame 4; frame 5 again has no reliable skeleton despite the very close foreground occluder. In frame 3, the detected hand lies slightly left and below the small yellow body joints, indicating an arm/hand extending toward the central hanging shirt at approximately arm’s reach, while the frame-4 hand is displaced rightward as the viewpoint or hand moves laterally. The compact joint patterns reveal articulated hand location and approximate orientation more clearly than RGB, but they are insufficient to establish a full person’s facing direction, gaze, exact distance, or spacing between people. Missing detections, compressed or anatomically implausible joints, and loss of the skeleton under strong occlusion make the map unreliable for body position outside frames 3–4.
